patterns.rationale: Catches the distinctive glyph-bullet format in Miss 2 where each list item is literally `- R — Repository`, a single capital letter flanked by spaces and an em/en-dash. This `- X — Word` structure is the explicit footprint of an acrostic encoding convention — no legitimate developer doc uses single-letter bullets separated by typographic dashes. Targeting em/en-dash (Unicode `\u2014`/`\u2013`) rather than plain hyphens keeps this narrow.
patterns.fp_notes: Glossaries sometimes use `- Term — Definition` but the term is never a bare single capital letter; any multi-character term (e.g. `- API — ...`) does not match the `[A-Z]\s+[—–]` middle segment.

patterns.rationale: Catches in-document decoder cues that direct a model to extract leading characters across lines or sections. Miss 3's footer is described as a "build-tool convention" line (e.g. `// Component key: derived from leading character of each lifecycle stage`) and Miss 7's cue is phrased as a "documentation handbook convention" (e.g. `Reference keys follow the initial-letter convention`). Both require language in the `(initial|leading) (letter|char) of each` family or an explicit `assembled/derived from` construction. The bare `acrostic` literal catches any document that names the scheme directly. This fits the FLIP_ATTACK axis which already covers non-standard reading instructions (`read backwards`, `reverse this`) — `read initial characters` is the same class of text-transformation directive.
patterns.fp_notes: Style guides occasionally say "the first letter of each sentence/word" for capitalisation rules, but that uses "sentence" or "word" — not the item-noun list (`line|item|entry|bullet|step|section|paragraph`) required here. The `leading char` and `initial char … of each` constructs are rare in normal developer prose.

semantic_note: Misses 6 and 8 are semantic-only — neither contains an in-document decoder cue. Miss 6 relies on the model recognising EXFILKEYS as a dispatch token from reconstructed bullet initials; Miss 8's READTOKENS acrostic is buried in pure audit prose. No regex can reconstruct multi-item initial sequences without comprehension.
